beats.question: What is it
beats.narration_text: I'm Varnika. I'm searching for a job myself, and reading hundreds of job postings by hand takes hours. So my final project is an agent that does the reading. It watches job boards, picks out the few postings that fit one person, and shows why each one made the list.

beats.question: Why it matters: most postings don't fit
beats.narration_text: Most postings don't fit. On October thirty-first, my written rules checked all six hundred and seventy-five postings on Anthropic's job board against a made-up candidate. Only one matched.

beats.question: A person decides
beats.narration_text: And it never acts on its own. It won't apply for jobs or send anything. It will hand a person the shortlist, and only that person can say yes, no, or not yet.

beats.narration_text: That matters because a tool that picks jobs for you should show its reasons, so you can check it, instead of just trusting it.

beats.question: Job alerts
beats.narration_text: What have other people done? The simplest tools are job alerts. LinkedIn and Indeed save your search, and send you new postings daily or weekly. But their help pages don't explain why a job matched.

beats.question: AI matching and auto-apply
beats.narration_text: Newer tools go further. LinkedIn's Skills Match compares your profile with the job description. Jobright says its agent matches roles and applies for you. LazyApply says its agent handles the entire application. Simplify's Autopilot submits with no review step, though its Copilot mode leaves the final click to you.

beats.question: Why mine still matters
beats.narration_text: So finding jobs is automated, and so is applying. None of these pages mentions rules you can recheck, a separate program that checks each run, or a person approving the shortlist. That's what mine adds.

beats.question: Where the data comes from
beats.narration_text: Here's how I'm building it. The data comes from public job board feeds that need no login: Anthropic on Greenhouse, Palantir on Lever, and Linear on Ashby. The candidate is made up, Aarav Patel, so no real person's data is used.

beats.question: Built so far: JS1
beats.narration_text: Two parts already work. In my first assignment, the agent watched one board, reported only new postings, and judged each one with five written rules: title, seniority, location, experience, and skills.

beats.question: Built so far: JS2
beats.narration_text: In the second, it became a loop over four boards on three systems, with a budget, and a permission policy in code that blocks any site not on its list. One run read one thousand and fourteen postings. It has a hundred and twenty-two tests, and a separate checker caught a real bug in one of my own runs.

beats.question: Next steps
beats.narration_text: Next, step by step. First, a filter I can read, with an audit of what it throws away, and the agent offered to Claude as a tool. Then a written plan before every run, a check on every claim, and memory across days. Last, the approval step, tied to the exact shortlist the person saw.

beats.narration_text: Do I have what I need? Yes. Python, with nothing to install. Claude Code, through my university. Free public job boards, and my laptop. No paid API credits are needed.

beats.question: Check 1: rejected postings
beats.narration_text: How will I know it worked? Four checks. One: I'll pull thirty postings the filter rejected, at random, and check each one by hand. If more than one of them fits the candidate, the filter failed.

beats.question: Check 2: must-skip list
beats.narration_text: Two: a test list of postings it must skip, like a closed posting, the wrong location, or one that only matches keywords. If even one gets through, that's a fail. And a healthy run should skip at least half of what it sees.
